title: Daily Production Report
body: The DPR gets read top to bottom for the total-movement line, which mostly looks fine — and that hides the real problems underneath it. At ADW, crusher stoppages logged as "bin level low" or "stockpile full" get treated as crusher issues when they're actually a load-and-haul sequencing failure, and that misread means the wrong fix gets ordered.
keyPoints: Read the report bottom-up, not top-down: general comments first (catches calendar/operational noise like roster breaks or blast cleanup before you misjudge a real miss), then the crusher downtime log, then excavator availability vs. utilization, then drilling variance last.

In the crusher downtime log, "bin level low" means the pit isn't feeding the crusher fast enough — a haul-sequencing problem, not a mechanical one. "Stockpile full" is the opposite fault: the pit is feeding fine but downstream (stockpile/plant) can't absorb it. Don't let both get logged as "crusher downtime" without distinguishing which one it is.

A wide gap between excavator availability and utilization (e.g., 96% available, 72% utilized) means the machines are fine and the loss is dispatch, sequencing, or haul-road condition — chasing mechanical causes wastes time when the fix is upstream of the machine.

Blast overspill at switchbacks and ramp edges has a real, repeatable cost: roughly 3 excavator-hours per cleanup event. Treat it as a line item, not background noise — it recurs enough to plan around.

An "ore ahead / waste behind" month looks like a win on the total line but is a sequencing signal: the fleet is stripping ore faster than planned while waste falls behind, and the surplus evaporates fast once the easy ore face runs out.
apply: If the crusher logs a stoppage on shift, check the reason code before assuming it's a mechanical or crusher-side fault — bin-level-low or stockpile-full both point back at the pit and dispatch, not the plant.
